title: UOCS. XVI. Census of post mass-transfer binaries across various evolutionary phases in M67

abstract: Diffuse interstellar bands (DIBs) are absorption features of uncertain origin observed in the optical and near-infrared spectra of stars and galaxies. Although their correlation with dust extinction is well established, the physical conditions governing their strength across different interstellar medium (ISM) environments remain poorly understood. We investigate the environmental dependence of the DIB $\lambda5780$ using spatially resolved MaNGA spectroscopy for 837 nearby galaxies spanning a broad range of stellar masses, star-formation rates, and ISM properties. Stellar and nebular parameters are derived via spectral fitting, while DIB absorption is measured from high-signal-to-noise spatially binned residual spectra. We detect the DIB $\lambda5780$ in 159 galaxies and report the most distant spatially resolved DIB detection to date, at 232 Mpc. The DIB $\lambda5780$ equivalent width correlates positively with both stellar and gas-phase extinction. DIB $\lambda5780$ is preferentially detected in regions of high extinction, near- or super-solar metallicity ($12+\log({\rm O/H})\gtrsim8.5$), and moderate specific star-formation rates ($-10.5\lesssim\log({\rm sSFR}/{\rm yr}^{-1})\lesssim-9$). By contrast, it falls below our detection threshold in metal-poor or strongly ionized environments. It is rarely detected in regions with little or no recent star formation, with the few detections in such environments occurring primarily in regions driven by composite ionization. Our results indicate that DIB $\lambda5780$ is preferentially detected, within the sensitivity limits of the MaNGA data, in dust-rich, chemically evolved, and moderately ionized environments.
comment: 12 pages of main text and 17 pages of appendices; 8 main-text figures and 20 appendix figures. Accepted for publication in MNRAS
title: Diffuse interstellar bands in nearby galaxies with MaNGA: environmental trends with metallicity, extinction, ionization, and star-forming activity

abstract: We have set up a simple experiment to characterise a dual-polarised bowtie dipole antenna at St. Stephens College as part of undergraduate radio astronomy experiments. The antenna provides two orthogonal linear polarisation responses, allowing us to investigate the polarisation properties of radio-frequency signals using a simple and affordable experimental setup. In this article, we present our analysis of the performance of the antenna and demonstrate its use through polarisation-rotation measurements. This antenna is part of the Sky Watch Array Network (SWAN) and this analysis helps us understand the response of each individual array element in the setup.
comment: 17 pages, 9 figures, 2 Tables
title: Performance Analysis of a Dual-Polarised Bowtie Antenna in the Low RF Band: A Low-Cost Undergraduate Laboratory Experiment

abstract: Successive type II solar radio bursts are often considered as diagnostics for the evolution of CME-driven shocks and their interaction with the structured solar corona. However, the physical mechanisms driving these successive type II emissions are not well understood, with prior studies mostly limited to single event. In this work, we provide the first statistical analysis of successive type II radio bursts over Solar Cycles 23, 24 and the ascending phase of Solar Cycle 25 (1997-2025). We have constructed a catalogue of 73 independent successive type II events using radio dynamic spectra and SOHO LASCO coronagraph observations. The events were divided into three observational classes, based on the inferred physical interaction mechanisms: CME-Streamer interaction, CME-CME interaction and Single-CME. Statistical analyses were performed on the 56 events with clear physical classification. CME-streamer interactions constitute the largest class among the physically classified event, highlighting the potential importance of the ambient coronal environment in shaping successive type II radio emission. Comparative statistical analyses indicate that the CME linear speed has marginal differences among the physical classes, but the CME angular width is significantly different between the CME-CME and CME-Streamer populations. Other factors, such as shock evolution and the ambient coronal environment, are important for the production of successive type II radio burst. The catalogue presented here provides a statistical framework for the investigation of CME-driven shock evolution.
comment: Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series, 20 Pages, 6 Figures, 5 Tables
title: Statistical Characterization of CME Interaction Responsible for Successive Type II Solar Radio Bursts

abstract: The Magellanic Stream (MS) is a gaseous structure extending over $150^\circ$ across the sky, likely formed through interactions between the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds (LMC and SMC) as they fell into the Milky Way (MW). Its predicted stellar counterpart would provide a collisionless record of these interactions, but few candidate members have been identified. To expand this sample, we constructed a catalog of 87,763 distant K-giant candidates using DELVE DR2 and VHS DR5 photometry and Gaia DR3 astrometry, and analyzed VLT and Magellan spectra of 51 targets along the trailing MS. Combining radial velocities, spectrophotometric distances, and proper motions, we identify five new MS candidates at 58--95 kpc. Their metallicities are consistent with the outskirts of the SMC, while orbit integrations in a time-dependent MW--LMC--SMC potential support a possible Magellanic origin. Combined with previously identified candidates, these stars span a substantially broader range of Magellanic latitude than predicted by existing models, suggesting an extended debris field rather than a narrow stream. The candidates also lie predominantly closer than the simulated debris. More recent, less eccentric SMC orbits may help explain this distance discrepancy, although new simulations are required to test their implications for the stellar debris, along with larger spectroscopic samples.
comment: 22 pages, 12 figures, submitted to ApJ
title: The Distant Milky Way Halo from the Southern Hemisphere: Spatially broad and closer stellar debris associated to the Magellanic Stream

abstract: The central regions of the Magellanic Clouds are crucial for understanding galaxy interactions and calibrating the cosmic distance scale, yet they remain observationally challenging due to extreme stellar crowding. We utilised deep VISTA observations (VMCDeep) to determine the highest-precision near-infrared Period-Luminosity (PL) and Period-Wesenheit (PW) relations to date for Classical Cepheids (delta Cep class, DCEPs) in the dense central regions of the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds (LMC and SMC). We analysed J and Ks time-series data covering the central 1.77 deg^2 of each galaxy. Utilising approximately 40 epochs per filter and PSF-based photometry, we derived high-quality light curves for 573 and 2090 DCEPs in the LMC and SMC, respectively. We derived exceptionally precise PL and PW relations, exhibiting the lowest photometric dispersion published so far for the Magellanic Clouds. Fourier parameters calculated from the light curves indicate that pulsational models incorporating a mildly non-canonical mass-luminosity relation and a mixing-length parameter of alpha = 1.7 best reproduce the observations. Age derivations confirm a bimodal star formation history in the SMC centre. Crucially, we discovered a striking line-of-sight spatial dichotomy within the young SMC DCEP population (t < 116 Myr), which is bifurcated into two distinct structures separated by ~4 kpc. This provides independent stellar evidence tracing a recent direct collision with the LMC. Finally, by unifying fundamental and first-overtone pulsators, we derived a highly constrained relative distance between the Clouds. Comparing this to detached eclipsing binary distances, our data suggest a moderate metallicity correction for the Leavitt Law with gamma ~ -0.2 mag/dex.
comment: Accepted for publication on A&A. 20 pages, 17 figures
title: VISTA Magellanic Clouds deep observations of Classical Cepheids: Precision distances and a collision-driven SMC

abstract: We present FOORT (Flexible Object-Oriented Ray Tracing), an open C++ code for ray-tracing images of black holes and other compact objects in arbitrary spacetimes. FOORT is designed to offer flexibility and can handle horizons, naked singularities and numerical metrics, allowing it to ray-trace numerous different metrics including Kerr and other black holes, as well as horizonless objects such as fuzzballs and boson stars. New metrics, analytical or numerical, can be added with minimal effort, and geodesics are initialized at the camera without reference to conserved quantities, so no special structure of the metric is required. Besides the intensity observed from a geometrically and optically thin equatorial disk, FOORT is set up to track a number of diagnostics along each geodesic, such as the number of equatorial crossings and the radius of closest approach. Its adaptive mesh can refine the image on any of these diagnostics, efficiently resolving narrow features such as higher-order photon rings. Accompanying Python tools convert the output into images and interferometric visibility amplitudes. We describe the main features of the code, validate it against analytic results in the Schwarzschild and Kerr spacetimes, demonstrate it on several non-Kerr metrics, and characterize its scaling with the number of OpenMP threads. FOORT is lightweight, requiring only C++17 and OpenMP, and has already been used in a number of studies of black hole and compact-object imaging. The code is publicly available in a GitHub repository.
comment: 31 pages, 11 figures
title: FOORT: Flexible Object-Oriented Ray Tracing

abstract: Many galaxy formation models represent supernova feedback by a continuous energy injection rate averaged over the stellar initial mass function (IMF). This approximation can fail in low-mass dark matter halos, where single, discrete supernovae can unbind more gas than the reservoir holds. We investigate this using a one-zone model that characterises continuous and discrete supernova feedback at redshifts $z\geq5$. Both feedback modes inject the same expected energy per unit stellar mass formed. In the discrete model, individual supernovae are resolved and energy is injected instantaneously; in the continuous model, supernovae are IMF-averaged and energy injection is spread over a finite time interval. Once stars form, a supernova can unbind 1.5-2.7 times the gas present. Continuous feedback begins removing gas after $\sim 4$ Myr, whereas the first discrete supernova occurs after $\sim 10$ Myr, which produces a stellar mass excess before feedback takes effect. The excess persists because the reservoir responds nonlinearly: an event removes at most the gas present, and star formation halts once it is empty. It depends strongly on halo mass: from 135 per cent at $10^7\, \rm{M}_\odot$, to 15 per cent at $10^8\, \rm{M}_\odot$, to negligible at $10^9\, \rm{M}_\odot$ by $z=5$. Fixing the number and timing of supernovae does not remove the stellar excess, which indicates that it is not caused by stochastic IMF sampling. Instead, it vanishes when the same energy is divided among more, smaller events. Matching the energy released per unit stellar mass therefore does not guarantee equivalent feedback in halos that retain gas until the first supernova.
comment: 15 pages, 7 figures; To be submitted to The Open Journal of Astrophysics; comments and feedback welcome
title: Discrete Supernovae and the Limits of Continuous Models in Low-Mass Dark Matter Halos

abstract: We study the geometric figures of neutron stars and magnetars with spin periods from milliseconds to seconds and magnetic fields from $10^{12}$-$10^{15}$ G to hypothetical values near the Chandrasekhar-Fermi virial scale, $10^{18}$ G. In Newtonian theory, we find the equilibrium figure of a rotating incompressible fluid with a current-free uniform interior magnetic field matched to an exterior dipole field by surface currents. For aligned axes, an oblate spheroid is obtained by minimizing the total gravitational, rotational and magnetic energy at fixed mass, volume, angular momentum and frozen magnetic flux. Its ellipticity is the sum of rotational and magnetic contributions, recovers the Ferraro limit for a weak magnetic field, and has a magnetic weight that depends on the eccentricity for large deformation. For misaligned magnetic and spin axes, we introduce a quadrupolar shape tensor and diagonalize it to find a triaxial ellipsoid whose principal axes are tilted by magnetic pressure. The tilt angle and eccentricities are computed analytically as functions of the rotational and magnetic eccentricities and the misalignment angle. The magnetic energy of the misaligned configuration is obtained in closed form in oblate spheroidal harmonics for arbitrary eccentricity and obliquity. Its weak-field deformation, up to $10^{15}$ G, is proportional to $P_2(\cosα)$, which fixes the magnetic forcing tensor, and its finite-eccentricity form gives a generalized Ferraro-Maclaurin relation for rotation-dominated misaligned stars. In the weak-field regime, the triaxial eccentricity is determined by the Ferraro eccentricity and the harmonic mean of order 2 of the rotational and magnetic eccentricities. The deformation parameters give the quadrupole moments and hence the continuous gravitational-wave amplitudes, luminosity and spin-down torque of the triaxial configuration.

title: Magnetically Deformed Neutron Stars and Gravitational Waves

abstract: Precise planetary mass measurements are essential for constraining the internal structure and envelope properties of exoplanets and to break key degeneracies in atmospheric retrievals. Estimating the observational effort needed to reach a desired mass precision is therefore fundamental for the optimisation of current and future radial velocity (RV) surveys. We present MINERVA, a tool designed to estimate the required number of RV observations to measure transiting planet masses to a given precision, providing a robust scheduling framework for large-scale samples. MINERVA simulates realistic RV time series for targets orbiting FGKM-type stars. The code ingests real-world observational timestamps to account for weather interruptions and seasonal visibility gaps. To model stellar activity, the pipeline draws ages from local neighbourhood distributions, uses empirical calibrations to derive rotation and magnetic activity levels, and translates these into time-varying RV signals. We also derived a new empirical calibration between chromospheric activity and RV dispersion for K-type stars, using Global Architecture of Planetary Systems (GAPS) and Ariel Mass Survey (ArMS) data. We validated MINERVA on targets with known planetary masses, yielding required observational efforts highly consistent literature values. To demonstrate its capabilities on statistically significant samples, we applied the code to a subsample of the Ariel Mission Candidate Sample. Adopting HARPS-N/TNG as the reference instrument, we estimated the observing nights necessary to achieve a 30% planetary mass precision, providing an optimised observational roadmap for atmospheric characterisation. MINERVA's probabilistic and flexible architecture allows the optimisation of ongoing RV campaigns, the evaluating of undersampling risks in active stars, and the dynamic guidance of population-wide characterisation strategies.
comment: 18 pages, 10 figures, accepted by A&A
title: Minimum observations for accurate Exoplanetary mass estimation with Radial Velocity Analysis (MINERVA)

abstract: Main-sequence B-stars with a strong magnetic field and moderately rapid rotation form centrifugal magnetospheres (CMs), which often exhibit distinct H$α$ line emission, as well as circularly polarized radio. For CMs of early-type B-stars with $T_{\rm eff} \gtrsim 17$ kK, the onset and strength of the H$α$ emission is well explained in terms of a centrifugal breakout (CBO) model, in which mass fed into the CM by the star's radiatively driven stellar wind builds up to a density that is sufficient for centrifugal forces to overwhelm magnetic confinement. The analysis here now argues that the observed diminution and disappearance of the H$α$ emission for CM B-stars with $T_{\rm eff} \lesssim 17$ kK can be explained by the failure of their lower luminosity to drive hydrogen-rich winds; instead they develop an ion runaway of heavier metal ions that are the seat of line-driving, which thus feed a metallic CM (mCM) for which the requisite hydrogen is diminished or even absent. For mid-B-type stars in a narrow transition range of effective temperature $T_{\rm eff} \approx (16.8 \pm 0.3)$ kK, hydrogen can still be driven to a sufficient speed to coast into the inner CM, which we show can explain the reduced strength and width of H$α$ line emission in the transition CM star $ρ$ Oph C. But even in regions with no hydrogen, the build-up of metal density to CBO levels can still drive the magnetic reconnection needed to produce the observed radio. We discuss whether such build-up of metals could give rise to direct observational signatures.
comment: 10 pages, accepted for publication in MNRAS
title: Low effective-temperature diminution of H$α$ emission from metallic centrifugal magnetospheres fed by ion-runaway winds

abstract: Radial surface brightness profiles (SBPs) and color gradients are useful tools for studying galaxy structure, formation, and evolution. While it is usually assumed that they are primarily driven by stellar properties, such as mass, age or metallicity, their dependence on 3D dust attenuation is not fully understood or accounted for. We analyze how 3D dust attenuation affects galaxy observations by hindering the estimation of intrinsic properties. We examine dust-induced shifts in surface brightness and color. Using SKIRT radiative transfer models, we simulated simple Sérsic galaxies, with spherically-symmetric stellar densities, constant stellar-to-dust ratios, and a spatially constant spectral energy distribution (SED). We find that attenuated SBPs differ significantly from dust-free profiles, particularly in the central galaxy regions. These differences become more pronounced at bluer wavelengths and for higher core dust densities, leading to variations in the fitted Sérsic index of up to ~25%. This can lead to incorrect conclusions about the intrinsic stellar distribution and mimic a central mass deficit. For galaxies with very centrally-dense dust distributions, a core-Sérsic model results in a better fit of the attenuated SBP. For dust masses as low as ~2*10^6 $M_{\odot}$, dust-induced negative color gradients reach the same order of magnitude as those commonly observed in galaxies, which a dust-screen fails to account for. This occurs even for a spatially invariant SED and can lead to wrong conclusions about intrinsic stellar populations and related astrophysical questions, such as their formation histories or the mechanisms of inside-out star formation quenching. A full 3D approach is necessary to properly model attenuation effects, which, if not accounted for, can bias inferences made about stellar populations, their evolutionary histories, and spatial distributions.
comment: 8 pages, 8 figures, submitted for publication to A&A
title: 3D dust attenuation effects in galaxies: structural biases and induced negative color gradients

abstract: We introduce the $r$-largest order statistics ($r$-LOS) framework for galaxy clusters, a generalization of the standard extreme value statistics (EVS) approach. While conventional EVS focuses on the probability distribution of the most massive cluster within a given volume, the $r$-LOS framework exploits the additional statistical information encoded in the joint distribution of the $r$ most massive clusters, ranked in descending order of mass. We develop the corresponding mathematical formalism, discuss its asymptotic properties, and derive a set of relations relevant to galaxy cluster cosmology. In particular, we demonstrate that the high-mass end of the halo mass function (HMF) can be reconstructed from the generalized extreme value (GEV) parameters inferred using an extension of the block maxima method that incorporates the $r$ most massive clusters in each volume. This provides a means of recovering the high-mass tail of the HMF using only a small subsample of the halo population. We validate these relations using both comoving and light-cone halo catalogues from numerical simulations. Finally, we investigate the sensitivity of the $r$-LOS framework to primordial non-Gaussianity, focusing on its impact on the statistics of massive clusters.
comment: 19 pages, 11 figures. Submitted to Physical Review D
title: $r$-Largest Order Statistics for Galaxy Cluster Cosmology I: Reconstruction of the high-mass end of the Halo Mass Function

abstract: The origin of dark matter is one of the major problems in modern cosmology. We can infer its existence from the gravitational potential wells around astrophysical objects, but there is no convincing explanation for what its nature and origin are. Moreover, experiments for direct detection, indirect detection, or particle production in accelerators have not shown, until now, any conclusive interaction between dark matter and particles in the standard model. This may imply that dark matter does not interact with ordinary matter and originates from pure gravitational interaction. In this manuscript, we investigate the possibility to constrain the gravitational production of dark matter from the 21cm brightness temperature at the cosmic dawn. Considering only the time when the absorption profile occurs, we can impose upper limits on the dark matter's mass. Future measurements have potential to extend current constraints and help understanding the nature of dark matter.
comment: 12 pages, 9 figures, 1 table
title: Constraining Dark Matter Gravitational Production with the 21cm Signal at the Cosmic Dawn

abstract: Combining galaxy clustering and weak gravitational lensing beyond two-point statistics offers a way to extract additional cosmological information while calibrating astrophysical nuisance parameters. We investigate this approach by combining 1-loop power spectra with tree-level bispectra, including all auto- and cross-bispectra of galaxy clustering and weak lensing, a combination that we refer to as $4\times3$pt by analogy with the well-known $3\times2$pt analysis. Modelling two- and three-point statistics consistently, with galaxy bias and intrinsic alignments described by the TATT model, we perform Fisher forecasts of dark energy constraints for a Euclid-like survey, with conservative scale cuts. When combined with CMB data, adding $4\times3$pt bispectra to the $3\times2$pt improves the dark energy figure of merit by about $30\%$, a gain that remains stable when using the three, four or five lowest redshift bins of our ten. To extend the analysis to ten tomographic bins, we compress the bispectra into skew-spectra, which improve the figure of merit by $20\%$ with the CMB and by $37\%$ without. We show that most of this improvement comes from the calibration of second-order galaxy bias parameters by three-point statistics, mainly by the galaxy-auto and the GGL bispectra. We also find that baryonic feedback is correlated with second-order intrinsic alignment parameters once the amplitude of the matter power spectrum is constrained by the CMB, and that bispectra reduce this correlation by calibrating intrinsic alignments, almost entirely through the GGL bispectra, a mechanism that could become more valuable with more flexible baryonic feedback models. These results demonstrate the potential of combined galaxy clustering and weak lensing bispectra to improve cosmological constraints from stage-IV galaxy surveys through the calibration of galaxy bias and intrinsic alignments.
comment: 44 pages, 9 figures
title: From $3\times2$pt to $4\times3$pt: calibrating galaxy bias and intrinsic alignments with galaxy clustering and weak lensing bispectra

abstract: Recently, the LHAASO Collaboration reported gamma-ray emission from the Peanut-shaped source (Peanut), which extends over $4.5^\circ$ parallel to the Galactic plane at $b=-17.5^\circ$. The source is associated with the millisecond pulsar PSR J0218+4232, located at the eastern edge of the Peanut, at a distance of 3 kpc from the Earth and 0.9 kpc from the Galactic plane. Its location and bright gamma-ray emission above 25 TeV make it a natural laboratory for studying the Galactic magnetic field (GMF) in the transition region between the Galactic plane and halo. We interpret the observed emission as inverse-Compton scattering of CMB photons by electrons propagating along the large-scale GMF, accounting for turbulence through two models: Kolmogorov and Goldreich-Sridhar (GS). These models correspond to diffusive and ballistic particle propagation, respectively. While the GS case naturally provides conditions for one-sided gamma-ray emission, in the Kolmogorov case assumptions of one-sided particle injection and magnetic mirror at the source are necessary. We find that, in the Kolmogorov scenario, the Peanut's hotspots are likely associated with magnetic bottling, whereas in the GS scenario, they are related to magnetic field line geometry. Both models yield constraints on the GMF at the location of the Peanut.
comment: 21 pages, 11 figures
title: LHAASO's Peanut source is a laboratory for studying magnetic fields in the Milky Way

abstract: In the standard cosmological model, the distribution of cold dark matter (CDM) can be reshaped by baryonic processes through gravity, as gas outflows alter the central potential and transform steep cusps into nearly constant-density cores. However, such feedback-generated cores are generally expected to have sizes comparable to the visible stellar body of a galaxy. Here we report the discovery of an exceptionally extended dark matter core in a nearby gas-rich dwarf galaxy UGCA 320. We combine high-resolution MUSE H$α$ kinematics in the inner region with high-, medium-, and low-resolution MeerKAT HI observations from the MHONGOOSE survey tracing the galaxy out to large radii. After accounting for an additional non-circular kinematic component identified in the central HI spectra, we construct an extended rotation curve to constrain the dark matter distribution. The resulting rotation curve is poorly reproduced by a cuspy Navarro-Frenk-White (NFW) halo but well described by cored pseudo-isothermal (ISO) and Burkert halo models. Consistently, a fit with a generalized NFW model yields an inner density slope of $γ=0.36\pm0.12$, quantitatively supporting a shallow central density profile. The best-fit ISO model gives a dark matter core radius of $7.62\pm0.80$ kpc, approximately four times the stellar half-light radius and substantially larger than typically found in dwarf galaxies. We investigate the main systematic uncertainties and find that the resulting core radii remain large, all lying within 3$σ$ of the fiducial fit. The exceptionally large core in UGCA 320 may pose a challenge to the standard CDM paradigm. While its properties are broadly consistent with self-interacting dark matter (SIDM), they may be difficult to reconcile with warm and fuzzy dark matter models, as well as the stellar feedback-driven core formation scenario.
comment: 25 pages,17 figures, 5 tables, submitted to Nature Communications
title: A giant dark matter core extending far beyond the stars of a dwarf galaxy

abstract: Gaia-4b is the first confirmed exoplanet discovered with Gaia astrometry, based on its identification as a possible exoplanet in the solution in Gaia Data Release 3 and subsequent confirmation with radial velocity. In this work we present a \texttt{python} framework called \texttt{pyGaiafits} that can jointly analyze astrometric time series and radial velocities. We use this to combine the precise along-scan astrometric time series for Gaia-4 from the Gaia DR4 pre-release with 44 radial velocities (RVs) obtained over three years from four independent spectrographs (HPF, HARPS-N, NEID, and FIES). By jointly fitting these two complementary datasets that collectively span a 12-year baseline ($\sim$7 orbital periods of Gaia-4b), we refine the system parameters and determine the true mass of Gaia-4b to be $10.70\pm0.32$~$M_J$. Critically, we do not find significant evidence for the long-term quadratic RV trend previously reported in the literature, recovering $\ddotγ = 5.5^{+8.3}_{-6.7}\;\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}\,yr^{-2}}$ consistent with zero. We discuss how this discrepancy likely arises from a degeneracy between orbital period and long-term trends when RVs span only $\sim$1.5 orbital cycles --- a degeneracy that is broken by anchoring the ephemeris with early Gaia astrometry.
comment: Accepted in AAS Journals. Code available here: https://github.com/shbhuk/pyGaiafits
title: A Joint Study of Epoch Astrometry and Radial Velocities of Gaia-4b

abstract: Solar filaments exhibit oscillatory motions in different directions, including large-amplitude longitudinal oscillations (LALOs), which are commonly interpreted as magnetoacoustic oscillations with gravity providing the main restoring force In the standard pendulum model, the magnetic-field geometry imposes an upper limit on the oscillation period of approximately 167 min near the solar surface. Here, we report a longitudinal oscillation observed in a solar filament using SDO/AIA 193 and 171 angstroms observations, with periods ranging from 178-184 min. These values are longer than the near-surface cut-off period derived under the assumptions of the standard pendulum model. To investigate this discrepancy, we consider two possible effects: the prominence height above the solar surface and the three-dimensional geometry of the magnetic field. The former increases the theoretical cut-off period by reducing the local gravitational acceleration, while the latter can modify the longitudinal restoring force through the inclination of the plane containing the local field-line curvature. Specifically, a locally concave-down field-line geometry can reduce the restoring force and permit longer periods, provided that the equilibrium remains stable. However, the available observations do not allow us to independently constrain the prominence height, field-line curvature, and inclination. This result highlights the importance of considering the three-dimensional geometry and curvature of filaments when interpreting their longitudinal oscillations. Since LALOs provide a potential seismological diagnostic for estimating the magnetic-field strength supporting filaments, neglecting their curvature may introduce systematic errors in such estimates. Therefore, accounting for the geometry of the oscillating structure is essential for the accurate application of filament seismology.
comment: 8 pages, 8 figures
title: Long-period longitudinal oscillations in a solar filament beyond the theoretical period limit

abstract: Stellar populations in the central regions of disc galaxies provide key constraints on their formation and secular evolution. We investigate the properties of young stellar populations in the centres of nearby barred galaxies from the TIMER survey, using four stellar population models, two based on empirical (MILES, X-Shooter) and two on theoretical (Starburst99, HR-pyPopStar) stellar libraries, complemented by independent gas-phase metallicities from emission-line diagnostics. The inferred stellar metallicities depend strongly on the adopted model. Measured as the 5th-to-95th percentile spread across the three galaxies analysed in detail, the empirical libraries recover variations of 1.11 and 0.98 dex, whereas the theoretical ones return 0.40 and 0.49 dex; the gas in the same regions spans 0.49 dex. Gas metallicities are indeed lower in the central star-forming regions, but the amplitude of that depression (about 0.3 dex in NGC 1097) exceeds what bar-driven inflow of disc gas can account for, given typical abundance gradients in literature. The age-metallicity relations consistently reveal two distinct components: an older population consistent with a self-enrichment scenario, and a younger population formed from gas inflows with a different chemical enrichment history. The empirical libraries produce a monotonic decline of metallicities from old to young populations, which would require a sustained inflow of metal-poor gas outpacing its own enrichment. The theoretical libraries instead recover a young component whose metallicity departs from the older populations only at the most recent ages and by a few tenths of a dex, compatible with a single dilution episode. Our results demonstrate that model choice critically affects inferred metallicities, with empirical stellar libraries recovering age-metallicity relations that demand physical conditions the gas measurements cannot sustain.

title: Model-dependent metallicities of young stellar populations in TIMER galaxies

abstract: Measuring the mass of the Milky Way is essential for understanding galaxy formation and evolution, characterizing the Galactic potential and assembly history, and probing the nature of dark matter. We derive the enclosed mass profile of the Milky Way out to Galactocentric distances of $\sim80\,\mathrm{kpc}$ using two halo tracers with full 3D kinematics: RR Lyraes (RRLs) and blue horizontal-branch stars (BHBs). Our sample consists of 7,550 RRLs and 8,230 BHBs constructed from the Large Sky Area Multi-Object Fiber Spectroscopic Telescope (LAMOST), the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS), and the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), spanning Galactocentric distances from $10$ to $100\,\mathrm{kpc}$. We estimate the enclosed mass using two independent methods: the spherical Jeans equation and the tracer mass estimator (TME). The two tracers yield consistent results, with $M(<81.7\,\mathrm{kpc}) = (4.76 \pm 0.23)\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$ from RRLs and $M(<82.8\,\mathrm{kpc}) = (4.66 \pm 0.35)\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$ from BHBs. Adopting an NFW profile to extrapolate the enclosed mass beyond the outermost radius probed by our tracers, we infer virial masses of $M_{200} = 8.12^{+0.72}_{-0.65}\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$ from RRLs and $M_{200} = 8.13^{+0.78}_{-0.67}\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$ from BHBs. We further validate our methodology using mock RRL and BHB samples constructed from two Auriga halos, finding that the inferred masses are underestimated by $15.5\%\pm2.8\%$ for RRLs and $11.9\%\pm3.4\%$ for BHBs, respectively. After correcting for these systematic errors, the Milky Way virial masses are $M_{200} = 9.79^{+0.93}_{-0.84}\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$ from RRLs and $M_{200} = 9.24^{+0.95}_{-0.84}\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$ from BHBs.

title: Measuring Milky Way Mass with RR Lyraes and Blue Horizontal Branch Stars

abstract: In this work we present a new approach to derive HII region metal abundances based on sulfur emission lines. We select M101 as benchmark galaxy to test our new methodology along the wide metallicity gradient of this huge face-on star-forming spiral. Based on previous studies, we compile a sample of 151 HII regions and compare their properties base on the galaxy radial profile. The new methodology is based on the derivation of the electron temperature of the double ionised sulfur, either by the direct measurement of the [SIII] auroral line or, at supersolar metalicities, from the $SO_{23}$ parameter. This new indirect method is able to extend the abundance gradient up to the very centre of the M101 galaxy (0.04 $R_e$). This new methodology mitigates systematic biases in direct abundance determinations based on auroral lines, while opening up new opportunities to improve commonly used strong line abundance calibrations in the intermediate to high metallicity regime.
comment: 12 pages, 10 figures, Submitted to Astronomy & Astrophysics
title: A new indirect approach for oxygen abundance determinations across a wide range of physical conditions

abstract: CUPID is a next-generation tonne-scale cryogenic experiment that will search for the neutrinoless double beta decay $(0νββ)$ of $^{100}$Mo. It will be located at the Gran Sasso National Laboratory (Italy) and will employ the cryogenic calorimetric technique to reconstruct the energy deposited in Li$_{2}$MoO$_{4}$ crystals, in which the isotope of interest is embedded. Preliminary measurements have been performed with the CUPID VSTT (Vertical Slice Test Tower), a prototype tower designed to test the detectors' response and the apparatus' mechanical and thermal stability. In addition, a key objective was to demonstrate the improved performance of germanium-based cryogenic light detectors. In CUPID, light detection is used for both particle identification and pile-up rejection. Li$_{2}$MoO$_{4}$ is a scintillating crystal, enabling particle identification by exploiting the dependence of light yield on particle type. This requires collecting the Li$_{2}$MoO$_{4}$ scintillation light, peaking at $\sim$600 nm, with a $\sim$300 $μ$m-thick high-purity germanium wafer placed next to the crystal. The wafer is also equipped with concentric Al electrodes biased at a few tens of volts. This bias improves the signal-to-noise ratio by an order of magnitude thanks to the Neganov-Trofimov-Luke effect. This work presents preliminary results on the performance of the VSTT light detectors and of its Optical Injection System.

title: Development of millikelvin scintillation photodetectors with CUPID

abstract: Axiodilatons provide a promising unified model of the Dark Sector whose properties are motivated by the use of accidental approximate symmetries to embed the light fields needed for observations into well-motivated UV physics in a technically natural way. These models turn out to help ameliorate many current puzzles in $Λ$CDM phenomenology (e.g. the Hubble tension and the evidence for evolving Dark Energy) `for free' despite not being designed for that purpose. We here explore in more detail another serendipitous feature of these models: their tendency to enhance early structure formation, in a way that seems suggestive given the accumulating evidence for structure arising earlier than expected in $Λ$CDM. Since early structure growth is the cleanest to study we explore in detail the expected 21cm signal produced by axiodilaton models, using the same parameter choices that improve agreement with observations elsewhere in cosmology. For fixed astrophysics, we forecast that SKA1-Low could distinguish dilaton couplings as small as a few times $10^{-2}$ from $Λ$CDM at $2σ$, mainly because of the earlier formation of structure. We provide complete derivations of the mass dependence of the relevant cosmological observables, including how dilaton-dependent baryon and electron masses affect the hyperfine transition, the Ly$α$ coupling, X-ray heating and ionization during cosmic dawn and the epoch of reionization. We provide details of radiative transfer, atomic physics and the equations governing the thermal and ionization state of the intergalactic medium.

title: Enhanced Early Structure from Axiodilatons & 21cm Observations

abstract: Foundation models are increasingly used across the sciences, but whether their internal computations correspond to known scientific operations or proceed through different mechanisms remains unclear. Understanding these mechanisms is essential for assessing reliability, identifying failure modes, and learning new science from the models. We present, to our knowledge, the first causal mechanistic interpretability study of an astronomy foundation model, AION-1, focusing on its multimodal advantage in redshift prediction, where combining imaging with photometry outperforms photometry alone. We find that this advantage is largest for spatially extended and dust-attenuated galaxies, and that most of it is localized to the first of the encoder's twelve blocks. Within that block, how well a property is linearly decodable does not predict whether it can be localized. Spatial extent is causally used, and one attention head dominates linear probing for it, yet ablating that head has negligible effect on redshift prediction: the information is distributed across heads and is decodable again one layer after we erase it. Dust attenuation shows the opposite pattern: it is only weakly decodable anywhere in the encoder, yet a single head is necessary for most of the multimodal advantage, particularly for the most dust-attenuated galaxies, and keeping that head as the only active head in its block preserves nearly all of the advantage. None of the astrophysically motivated operations we tested explains what this head computes. Whether this reflects a limitation of current interpretability methods or a computation that does not correspond to any known astrophysical operation remains open, and resolving it is a prerequisite for using interpretability as a tool for scientific discovery.

title: A Mechanistic Interpretability Study of an Astronomy Foundation Model

abstract: The triple-exchange bispectrum of the scalar quasi-single-field inflation model has resisted analytic evaluation across its full parameter space since its advent, despite rapid progress in cosmological collider physics. In this Letter, we solve it for general mass and mixing strength as a convergent double series, by applying the Mellin-Barnes representation directly to the mixed propagator between the massless and massive modes. The result is exact, non-perturbative, and physically transparent; the method is broadly applicable.
comment: 9 pages
title: Triple-Massive-Exchange Bispectrum of Quasi-Single-Field Inflation

abstract: Energy-deposition fluctuations determine the isotope-separation capability of multilayer silicon detectors. We measure the central peak widths of $^{124}$Xe signals in 300- and 675-micrometre silicon layers at incident energies of approximately 152-274 MeV per nucleon and compare them with Geant4 11.4.0 electromagnetic option 4 (emopt4) and a calculation with explicit charge exchange. In the 300-micrometre detector, the emopt4 relative width of 1.844% exceeds the unselected experimental width of 1.407% by 31% and the selected width of 1.060% by 74%. For the 675-micrometre detector, selection windows around the downstream-signal peak, each approximately ten fitted first-plane standard deviations wide, give experimental upper estimates of 0.66-0.74%, compared with emopt4 predictions of 1.01-1.24%. Explicit charge-state transport gives widths of 0.889-0.932% for the thinner layer, depending on the incident charge distribution, and 0.59-0.63% for the thicker layer. These predictions are consistent with the experimental upper estimates, while emopt4 overestimates the widths for both thicknesses throughout the studied energy interval.
title: Xenon energy-deposition widths in silicon: measurements and Geant4 comparisons

abstract: Compound lensing in double-source-plane lenses (DSPLs) introduces multiple mass-sheet transformations that bias the inferred distance ratios $β$ used to constrain cosmology. We present the recovered $β$ from lens models of simulated compound lenses and explore the systematic biases that arise from a mass-sheet transformation in the first source plane. We examined simulated observations based on SDSS J0946+1006, in which we varied the matter distribution of source 1. We found a strong correlation between the stellar-to-halo mass and the recovered $β$. We produced a simulated catalogue of DSPLs detectable by the Euclid telescope to see if the same systematic propagates to a more varied population. But at Euclid's resolution, the properties of source 1 were poorly constrained, and any correlated bias was lost in the statistical uncertainty. We inferred $w_0$ and $Ω_{\rm m}$ for a flat $w$CDM cosmology from our $β$ posteriors for our combined sample. We found the cosmology biased when using the full mock Euclid sample, but reduced the bias substantially using a limited, well-modelled ''gold'' sub-sample, bringing it to within $\sim2σ$ and $\sim1σ$ of the ground-truth cosmology for simulated Euclid and Hubble Space Telescope imaging, respectively. Therefore, we must eliminate systems with unreliable lensing information, and for extreme compound lensing, the model complexity must be sufficient to reproduce the lensing observations. DSPLs remain a promising cosmological probe that could provide independent and complementary constraints to existing probes.

title: Can we constrain cosmology with compound gravitational lenses?

abstract: Highly spinning binary black holes exhibit complex inspiral dynamics and offer a powerful opportunity to probe gravity in a stronger-field and more dynamical regime than non-spinning binaries. Gravitational-wave signals from such systems enable stringent parameterized tests of deviations from the source dynamics predicted by general relativity. We show that highly spinning, mass-asymmetric binaries can provide enhanced sensitivity to deviations entering at higher post-Newtonian orders, which remain comparatively poorly constrained. Using NR simulations from the SXS catalog, we first recover the injected signals within general relativity using $\texttt{IMRPhenomXPHM-SpinTaylor}$, $\texttt{IMRPhenomXPNR}$, and $\texttt{SEOBNRv5PHM}$, finding model-dependent biases in the inferred masses, spins, and spin orientations. We then analyze the same signals with the $\texttt{IMRPhenomXPHM}$-based inspiral parameterized test of general relativity framework, TIGER, and find that these waveform-systematic biases can lead to apparent deviations from general relativity, which become significant for loud signals. Our results highlight that highly spinning binaries offer powerful tests of higher-order post-Newtonian deviations, but waveform inaccuracies can lead to false signs of new physics.
comment: 20 pages, 8 figures
title: Highly spinning binary black holes: promise and pitfalls for parameterized tests of general relativity

abstract: Stellar magnetic activity is known to decrease as stars age, but the underlying physical mechanism for this decline remains a key question. Does this evolution occur because individual starspots become magnetically weaker (a change in quality), or because the total area covered by spots diminishes (a change in quantity)? We address this question by synthesizing results from two recent studies that leverage starspot transit mapping of Kepler and CoRoT targets. First, we show that the magnetic field strength of starspots remains consistently high, on a saturation plateau of approximately 3500 G, regardless of stellar age or rotation period. This suggests that the intrinsic quality of spots does not significantly evolve. Second, we demonstrate a strong anticorrelation between starspot area coverage and stellar age, with young stars exhibiting large filling factors (up to 29%) that decrease sharply over time. Our combined results provide compelling evidence that the evolution of stellar magnetic activity is primarily driven by a change in the quantity of magnetic flux emerging on the surface, not by a change in the intrinsic strength of the spots themselves. These findings have direct implications for refining stellar dynamo models and improving age-dating techniques.
comment: 7 pages, 3 figures. Published in Proceedings IAU Symposium No. 400, "Solar and Stellar Multi-scale Activity", S. Vargas-Domínguez & J. C. Buitrago-Casas, eds., 2026, pp. 122-128
title: Unraveling the Magnetic Fields of Starspots with Transit Mapping

abstract: The distance duality relation links luminosity and angular diameter distances under standard photon propagation. It is usually tested by combining distances from different probes, which requires matching their redshifts and assuming sky isotropy. Self-sufficient probes, which measure both distances for the same object, avoid the first requirement and make the second testable. We assess whether quasars can serve as such probes, combining luminosity distances from the UV--X-ray relation with angular diameter distances from spectroastrometry and reverberation mapping (SARM). As a proof-of-concept, we apply the test to the quasar Mrk~509 and find $η\equiv d_{\rm L}/[(1+z)^2d_{\rm A}] = 0.50^{+0.61}_{-0.27}$, consistent with no violation at $0.8σ$. We then forecast the number of quasars needed to detect a constant and a linearly redshift-dependent violation, motivated by the findings of Teixeira et al. (2025) with potential implications for the Hubble tension and dark energy. A constant violation, $α_0=-0.075$, equivalent to a recalibration of the SNIa distance scale, could be detected at $3σ$ with 274--840 quasars. Since SARM distances, unlike BAO, do not rely on early-time physics, this would separate an early-time origin of the Hubble tension from a SNIa miscalibration or a distance duality violation. The redshift dependence is harder to detect: 1000 quasars would exclude $η=1$ at $3.4$--$6.6σ$, but detecting the dependence itself requires $2.6\times10^4$--$8\times10^4$. GRAVITY+ could bring quasar tests of a constant violation within reach.
comment: 10 pages, 2 figures. Comments are welcome
title: Quasars as a self-sufficient probe of the distance duality relation

abstract: Extreme mass-ratio inspirals (EMRIs) consist of a stellar-mass compact object orbiting a massive black hole and are among the primary targets for the future space-based gravitational-wave detector LISA. Their orbital eccentricity carries valuable information about their astrophysical origins, making its detection particularly important. However, increasing eccentricity has competing effects on detectability: it makes eccentric waveforms easier to distinguish from circular ones, but also redistributes signal power across multiple harmonics, reducing the power captured by single-harmonic searches. In this work, we quantify this trade-off within a semi-coherent framework for a source with fixed total SNR of $50$. Eccentricity becomes distinguishable from zero for final eccentricities $e_f \gtrsim 0.05$, while single-harmonic sensitivity declines beyond $e_f \simeq 0.1$. In noise-free analyses, including enough harmonics to recover at least $50\%$ of the total SNR avoids this degradation, but adds statistical freedom when calibrating detection thresholds. We apply the framework to two astrophysical EMRI populations, showing how these competing effects interact with their eccentricity distributions under simplified assumptions. The balance among eccentricity-driven distinguishability, harmonic power loss, and the statistical cost of additional harmonics is an important consideration for future EMRI search developments.
comment: Submitted to Physical Review D. 30 pages, 20 figures
title: Eccentricity detectability in Extreme Mass-Ratio Inspirals

abstract: A 35.6\,deg$^2$ field of Euclid Data Release~1 that covers part of the corona and tidal tails of the young (100--130\,Myr) nearby (234\,pc) open cluster Blanco~1 is presented. We select 22 ultracool dwarfs from Euclid photometry and slitless spectra, and measure proper motions over a median baseline of 13\,yr by combining Euclid astrometry with VIKING, KiDS and Rubin positions. Ten objects are comoving late-M and L dwarf candidates with membership probabilities of at least 0.5 under two field models. Nine of them are typed from their Euclid spectra, and the tenth is a candidate only if its colour-based type is adopted. Brown dwarf evolutionary models give masses of 0.03--0.06\,$M_\odot$ for the cluster age. The substellar population is about twice that predicted by a lognormal mass function scaled to the cluster's Gaia members. The remaining 12 objects are classified as late-M, L and T dwarfs with low probability of membership in the cluster. Using the Euclid sample to calibrate a search over 246\,deg$^2$ of VIKING and KiDS photometry and motions, we identify 60 ultracool candidates, with about seven expected by chance. In the core region of Blanco 1 archival Subaru Hyper Suprime-Cam images and motions over 2011--2025 yield 35 candidates of types M7 or later, at least 20 of which are kinematic members at 95\% confidence. These results extend the spectroscopic sequence of Blanco 1 into the L-type brown dwarfs and the list of candidate members over the outskirts and tidal tails of the cluster.

title: Euclid DR1 Legacy Science on Ultracool Dwarfs: Brown Dwarfs in the Blanco 1 Open Cluster

abstract: CCGeant4 models energy-loss fluctuations of heavy ions in Geant4, accounting for both charge exchange and relativistic corrections to electron scattering beyond the first Born approximation. We use GLOBAL cross sections for electron capture and loss, ATIMA equilibrium stopping powers and charge-dependent delta-electron spectra calculated from the Dirac equation in a frozen-shell potential. The package also supports tabulated elastic ion-nucleus scattering. The silicon example includes interference between Coulomb and nuclear scattering amplitudes. We compare charge evolution with GLOBAL and energy-loss spectra with MOCADI for matched beams and targets. Experimental comparisons cover the energy-loss measurements of Weick et al. and several measurements of energy deposited by xenon ions in silicon. For uranium at 800 MeV/u, the energy-loss variances from our Dirac configuration agree with the screened-ion calculations of Weick et al. to within 4% in Be, Al and Pb. Both calculations lie within the reported experimental uncertainties for all three targets, while calculated bismuth spectra in silver are narrower than measured. Calculations in thin silicon layers show that delta-electron escape can make deposited-energy distributions substantially narrower than primary-ion energy-loss distributions, highlighting the importance of secondary-electron transport for detector-response modelling. The distribution includes the Geant4 source patch, the transport tables and their converters, and a runnable example.
title: CCGeant4: charge-state-resolved transport and energy-loss fluctuations of relativistic heavy ions in Geant4

abstract: Extension of high performance optical frequency comb-based time transfer to real-world systems is challenged by platform motion, particularly for large relative velocities. Here, we utilize agile electro-optic frequency combs to construct a laboratory-based simulator of a two-way optical time transfer system under motion. Through direct control of the electro-optic frequency comb parameters, we can artificially induce the effects of relative motion. We performed tests of the time transfer performance across a km-scale fiber link for velocity profiles that linearly increase from rest up to 400 m/s. Through a post-processed data analysis, we demonstrate continuous tracking of the clock offset between sites with subpicosecond precision throughout the velocity sweep. These results illustrate the versatility of using electro-optic frequency combs for optical time transfer in deployed systems.
title: Subpicosecond Optical Time Transfer under Simulated Motion with Electro-Optic Frequency Combs

abstract: Identifying pre-flare magnetic conditions that determine whether a flare will be eruptive (associated with a coronal mass ejection) or confined remains a major challenge in solar physics. Motivated by previous statistical results showing that some eruptive flares occur under ideal MHD-stable conditions, we investigate the roles of kink instability (KI), torus instability (TI), preflare reconnection traced by precursor brightenings (PBs) and magnetic nonpotentiality in solar eruptiveness using an expanded sample of 68 flares above GOES class M4 from 2011--2024. To characterize the nonpotentiality of each active region (AR), we calculate the relative helicity $H_R$, current-carrying helicity $H_J$ and free magnetic energy. We find that, (1) 17 of 18 TI-unstable events and 12 of 19 KI-unstable events are eruptive, indicating that the TI parameter outperforms the KI parameter (2) although PBs are more commonly found in the MHD-unstable regime, only 3 of the 12 eruptive events in the TI/KI-stable regime show PBs, suggesting that preflare reconnection may play a secondary role compared with other factors. (3) The strongest indicator of eruptiveness is obtained by combining the TI parameter with magnetic nonpotentiality. Specifically, 24 of 36 eruptive flares satisfy $\sqrt{\left| H_J \right|}/φ\geq 0.1$ or $n \geq 1.13$, whereas 24 of 25 confined flares satisfy $\sqrt{\left| H_J \right|}/φ\le 0.1$ and $n \le 1.13$, where $φ$ is the total unsigned magnetic flux and $n$ is the decay index. These results suggest that the overall magnetic environment of ARs may play a significant role in determining the eruptiveness, in addition to the effect of MHD instability and reconnection.
comment: 10 pages, two tables, accepted by ApJ
title: The Role of Precursors and MHD Instabilities in Distinguishing Confined and Eruptive Solar Flares

abstract: In the era of high-precision Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) anisotropy measurements, detection of primordial gravitational waves (PGWs) is one of the main goals of current CMB experiments. Detection of a divergence-free ($B$-mode) component in CMB polarisation will provide direct evidence of inflationary PGWs in the early universe. However, weak gravitational lensing of CMB photons due to intervening mass distribution of the Universe distorts the primordial polarisation patterns, introducing an additional lensing-induced $B$-mode signal. Removing these lensing-induced $B$-modes is essential for improving constraints on the amplitude of PGWs. In this work, we present a multi-tracer delensing analysis using simulations of the Rubin Observatory LSST galaxy catalogue and Simons Observatory (SO) CMB maps. We use realistic photometric redshift errors for LSST mock catalogue and high complexity Galactic foregrounds for CMB simulations. By adopting a tomographic multi-tracer approach that combines the CMB and LSST mock data, we achieved a 10-20% higher delensing efficiency compared with using CMB data alone. Our analysis removes approximately 60% of the lensing-induced $B$-mode power. We find that photometric redshift errors in the mock galaxy catalogue introduce biases in the inferred galaxy bias and $σ_{8,0}$ parameters. However, these uncertainties do not produce a significant systematic bias in the inferred tensor-to-scalar ratio.
comment: under review in A&A journal
title: Improved delensing of CMB $B$-modes with upcoming SO and LSST Year-1 mock dataset: Impact of photometric redshift errors

abstract: Axion inflation, in which a pseudoscalar inflaton couples to a $U(1)$ gauge field via a Chern-Simons interaction, has garnered significant interest due to its rich phenomenology. The power spectrum and bispectrum for this model are often parametrized by functions known as $f_2$ and $f_3$, respectively. Previous work computed $f_2$ and $f_3$ using an approximation for the gauge field mode functions. While these approximate solutions are fairly accurate ($\mathcal{O}(10\%)$) for large values of the model parameter $ξ$, which controls gauge field particle production, our recent work has shown them to be quite inaccurate for smaller values of $ξ$. We present new fitting functions for $f_2$ and $f_3$ that are significantly more accurate than those previously used. We use these functions to place new constraints on $ξ$ and also set lower bounds for the energy scale of the axion gauge field coupling for $φ^{1/3}$ and $φ^{2/3}$ inflationary potentials. Additionally, we present a new public code to efficiently generate realizations of the primordial curvature perturbation for axion inflation in the weak backreaction regime. This code enables numerical computation of higher order correlators and provides a novel path to initial conditions for large-scale structure formation.
title: Improved constraints on axion inflation with the new code AxioGen: an efficient generator of curvature perturbations

abstract: The traditional method to measure Type-1 Active Galactic Nuclei central black hole masses ($M_{BH}$) is the reverberation mapping (RM) technique. Motivated by the desire to find a less observationally expensive method (than RM) to estimate $M_{BH}$, we have explored a purported correlation between X-ray luminosity and $M_{BH}$. For this we have compiled a sample of 35 AGN with RM $M_{BH}$ estimates that were detected in the eROSITA All-Sky Survey public data release. Using a sample that is larger than that of J. A. Mayers et al. 2018 and has a cleaner selection function, we confirm their XMM-Newton based result of a positive correlation. However, the scatter on the scaling relation remains too high ($σ_\mathrm{int}=0.50^{+0.08}_{-0.06}$) to make this a practical method to predict $M_{BH}$ for a given X-ray detected Type-1 AGN. That said, our findings can be used to improve mock X-ray skies generated from large volume hydrodynamical cosmological simulations. Such mocks are a necessary ingredient for cluster cosmology and preparation for future missions such as NewAthena.
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure
title: Exploring a Correlation Between AGN Black Hole Mass and X-ray Luminosity

abstract: We study the theory and signatures of a Mirror Twin Higgs (MTH) scenario in which stable twin neutrons constitute most of the dark matter (DM), while a subdominant component of twin elements survives as nuclear atomic dark matter (naDM). This framework offers a solution to the $matter~coincidence~problem$ ($Ω_{\rm DM}\simeq5Ω_b$), as the twin $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry can correlate the visible and DM mass scales and their number densities. We analyze twin nucleon freeze-out and the onset of twin Big Bang nucleosynthesis (BBN) to estimate the total naDM abundance, and determine which elements in the dark periodic table could be populated. An appreciable but subdominant naDM component generally requires a fractional nucleon mass splitting near the percent level, with twin-BBN creating heavy elements up to twin carbon. Strong twin neutron-proton scattering allows nearly all of the dark matter, not only the atomic sub-component, to participate in $dark~acoustic~oscillations$ (DAO) at early times, giving rise to a characteristic two-stage DAO signature that may be detected with future cosmological probes. Interactions between the twin and visible sectors, including the irreducible Higgs portal, make this scenario a well-motivated target for future directional direct-detection searches, and the naDM sub-component is expected to exhibit highly exotic astrophysics. We outline a supersymmetric twin Froggatt-Nielsen realization in which spontaneous $\mathbb{Z}_2$ breaking in the flavon sector can generate the required fermion spectrum and Higgs potential.
comment: 83 + 16 pages + Refs., 19 Figures, 4+2 Tables
title: The Dark Side of the Periodic Table: Theory and Signatures of Nuclear Atomic Dark Matter

abstract: The dynamical evolution of globular clusters is significantly influenced by the multiscale structure introduced by the presence of multiple stellar populations. In this study, we investigate the long-term dynamical evolution of the stellar mass function (MF) within globular clusters hosting two stellar populations using a suite of Monte Carlo simulations run with the MOCCA code. Dynamical processes including two-body relaxation, mass segregation, and tidal stripping result in distinct radial profiles describing the variation with distance from the cluster's center of the stellar MF slope within the first population (P1), the second population (P2), and the cluster as a whole. We show that these radial profiles are well described by a broken power law with a knee located slightly interior to the half-mass radius, a feature partially driven by the multiscale structure of the multiple populations. In both 3D and 2D projected coordinates, we explore several characteristic clustercentric distances within the profile, including those where the local MF slope matches the global value of the present-day MF slope and the initial mass function (IMF) slope, and we examine how these positions evolve with the cluster's dynamical age. Our results highlight how the initially more centrally concentrated P2 drives a steeper radial gradient and a steeper MF slope in the outer regions, which subsequently affects the global cluster values. Motivated by recent observational studies suggesting that a bottom-light IMF may better describe massive globular clusters, as well as measurements of a flatter P2 MF slope in the outer regions of 47 Tucanae, we additionally explore a three-parameter bottom-light IMF and a simulation in which the P1 IMF differs from the P2 IMF, with the P2 IMF flatter than that of the P1 in the lower mass range.
comment: 13 pages, 18 figures, accepted for publication in A&A
title: Dynamical evolution of the stellar mass function in multiple-population globular clusters

abstract: Cosmic rays (CRs) accelerated by the first supernovae could heat the intergalactic medium (IGM) before reionization. Previous 21-cm simulations, assuming a kinetic-energy power-law spectrum and simplified galaxy populations, found that CR heating can rival X-ray heating from high-mass X-ray binaries, imprint a distinct signature on the 21-cm power spectrum, and flatten the absorption trough of the global 21-cm signal. Here we model CR heating in 21cmFAST with: (i) the momentum power-law spectrum predicted by diffusive shock acceleration; (ii) Coulomb losses off free electrons; and (iii) injection from data-informed populations of atomic-cooling and molecularly cooled galaxies. We find that CR heating is about an order of magnitude weaker than previously estimated because a momentum power law places little energy in the sub-relativistic protons ($\lesssim 40$ MeV) that supply 99% of the heat. For our fiducial spectral slope, at the hard end of those inferred for Galactic supernova remnants, and for matched efficiency, this reduces the heating by a factor of $\approx 12$, and together with a more realistic galaxy model, by a factor of $\approx 28$ at $z = 15$. At the efficiencies that supernovae can supply, CR heating is weaker than standard X-ray heating, and the global signal alone cannot tell the two apart. Distinguishing CR from X-ray heating with the 21-cm power spectrum requires CR efficiencies a few times higher than those expected from local observations. At such efficiencies, CR heating yields up to $\approx 55\%$ more power than X-ray heating at matched global signal (median over scales), compared with only 3-6% at a locally motivated efficiency. A flattened absorption trough, like the one claimed by EDGES, requires efficiencies over two orders of magnitude above the local ones, beyond plausible Population III supernova budgets.
comment: 33 pages, 9 figures. Submitted to JCAP
title: Cosmic Ray Heating of the Early IGM: Realistic Galaxy Populations, Reduced Efficiency, and 21-cm Signatures

abstract: We study cosmological perturbations sourced by metastable domain wall (DW) networks. Using the unconnected segment model, we derive analytic expressions for the scalar and tensor power spectra in the long-wavelength regime, finding a fixed ratio between their amplitudes during the scaling regime. These spectra grow as the network evolves, driven by the increasing correlation length and slower redshifting of the wall energy density relative to radiation, and peak at a scale set by the network's collapse time. Comparing the scalar spectrum with observational constraints, we derive bounds on the DW energy density at collapse, which we apply to $\mathbb{Z}_2$ and axion models. When these bounds are saturated, the resulting CMB $B$-mode signal can be comparable to or larger than the inflationary signal for a tensor-to-scalar ratio $r \sim 0.03$, potentially bringing it within reach of future CMB polarization experiments.

title: Cosmological Signals from Finite-Lifetime Domain Wall Networks

abstract: Omega Centauri ($ω$ Cen; NGC 5139), the likely stripped nucleus of a dwarf galaxy accreted by the Milky Way, is one of the few galactic nuclei resolvable into individual stars. Because of its long relaxation time, the kinematics of its stars may still retain memory of how this nucleus formed. We combine HST proper motions and MUSE line-of-sight velocities from the oMEGACat survey to compare populations defined by abundance variations (the chromosome map), metallicity, and age within the half-light radius. The chromosome-map division separates two dynamically distinct components. The primordial stars have a flattened dispersion field, with kinematic ellipticity $ε\approx 0.7$ ($σ_{\rm minor} / σ_{\rm major} \approx 0.8$), which we recover independently in the line-of-sight velocities and the proper motions. The enriched stars are consistent with $ε=0$ in the line-of-sight velocities and are no more flattened than the full sample in the proper motions, and the two components show no strong difference in rotation. Metallicity bins show no comparable structure, because each bin mixes stars from both components, and the age-metallicity sample covers only the cluster core, where it cannot test for the flattening. The present-day central concentration of the most enriched (P2) stars suggests that they formed more centrally concentrated than the primordial stars, independent of assembly scenario. These results favor a picture in which the primordial stars retain the flattened orbital structure of the progenitor, while the enriched stars fell inward as dense clumps or formed in compact, centrally concentrated starbursts.

abstract: Atom interferometers are sensitive to oscillations of the masses and transition frequencies of atoms, which can be induced by axion dark matter. The main limitation is the sensitivity to gravity gradient noise (GGN). We propose a dual-species atom interferometry sequence that provides a suppression of GGN by up to three orders of magnitude and a sensitivity enhancement via the mass difference of the two atoms. We show that, under realistic experimental assumptions, a 10m-baseline dual-species atom interferometer is more sensitive to the axion gluon coupling than a 100m single-species gradiometer. Including a comprehensive noise analysis, we demonstrate that the Very Long Baseline Atom Interferometer (VLBAI) in Hannover with a baseline of 10m can probe the axion decay constant at levels almost competitive with leading laboratory constraints. The proposed 100m-baseline Atom Interferometer CERN Experiment (AICE) can extend this sensitivity by up to two orders of magnitude, surpassing laboratory constraints for axion masses of $10^{-19}\;\text{eV}/c^2 \lesssim m_a \lesssim 3\times10^{-15}\;\text{eV}/c^2$.

title: Dual-species atom interferometry for axion dark matter

abstract: We investigate the effects of cubic curvature corrections on the shadows of rotating black holes within the effective field theory of gravity. Starting from a perturbatively corrected Kerr metric incorporating two independent cubic curvature couplings, we construct black hole shadows through numerical integration of null geodesics, without assuming separability of the geodesic equations. Using a Hamiltonian ray-tracing approach, we systematically examine the dependence of the shadow geometry on the higher-curvature couplings, black hole spin, and observer inclination. We find that cubic curvature interactions can produce discernible deviations from the Kerr shadow, modifying its apparent size and shape. In particular, the two cubic interactions exhibit distinct effects on the shadow boundary, with the magnitude of the deviations depending sensitively on the coupling strengths and black hole spin. We validate our numerical results through independent convergence tests of the geodesic integration and shadow-boundary determination, and recover the analytical Kerr shadow in the vanishing-coupling limit. Our results provide a complementary probe of higher-curvature gravity in the strong-field regime and illustrate the potential of black hole shadow observations to constrain departures from general relativity.

title: Cubic Curvature Deformations to the Kerr Black Hole Shadow

abstract: The Euclid mission is revolutionising the study of strong gravitational lenses by providing high-resolution imaging over an unprecedented survey area, increasing the number of known lenses by two orders of magnitude compared to previous surveys. Characterising this sample of lens-galaxies requires accurate measurements of their physical properties. However, standard catalogue photometry often blends the light from the foreground lens and the lensed background source, limiting the reliability of derived galaxy parameters. We present a homogeneous catalogue of photometric redshifts and physical properties for 9538 galaxy-scale strong lenses identified in Euclid's DR1 strong-lens sample. We use deblended multiwavelength photometry obtained from the lens modelling of Euclid and ground-based images with PyAutoLens. The photometric redshifts of the lens galaxies are estimated using the template-fitting code Phosphoros. The stellar masses, SFRs, stellar ages, and metallicities are inferred through SED fitting with Prospector, adopting a flexible non-parametric SFH and a Salpeter IMF. The robustness of the inferred parameters is assessed through comparisons with spectroscopic redshifts and external galaxy surveys. The sample of lenses spans a broad redshift range of $0.13\lesssim z_{\rm phot} \lesssim 1.98$, with a median $z_{\rm phot} = 0.68^{+0.33}_{-0.29}$. The sample is dominated by massive quiescent galaxies with a $M_\ast$ range $[10^{10},\,10^{12.1}]\,M_\odot$ and a median $\log_{10}(M_\ast/M_\odot) = 11.39^{+0.29}_{-0.33}$. This catalogue represents one of the first large-scale characterisations of strong-lens galaxies in the Euclid era. By combining deblended photometry with homogeneous photometric redshift and SED-fitting analyses, it provides a foundation for studies of galaxy evolution, lens-galaxy scaling relations, and the connection between stellar and total mass in strong lenses.

abstract: Quantum sensor networks can use the spatial phase coherence of wavelike dark matter to probe not only particle properties but also the motion and structure of the Galactic halo. We explore this idea for the minimal two-node network, in which a nonlocal exchange measurement samples the characteristic function of the velocity distribution. We compare the Standard Halo Model (SHM) with a Gaia-inspired radially anisotropic component and their mixture (SHM++), taking into account daily and annual modulation, postselection, depolarizing events, and a flat instrumental offset. We show that annual modulation at one fixed local sidereal time has the same phase waveform for the centered SHM and Gaia-inspired SHM++ models, leaving them degenerate when the overall signal amplitude is unknown. Earth's rotation breaks this degeneracy by scanning the baseline through Galactic directions and exposing the direction-dependent coherence of an anisotropic population. Distinguishing these velocity distributions would test whether the local halo is smooth and nearly isotropic or contains a radially biased accreted component, turning a quantum-network detection into a probe of Milky Way structure. Our likelihood analysis shows how modulation and signal-odd controls separate this information from flat backgrounds and provides a path from model discrimination toward measurement of the local velocity distribution.

abstract: The Magellanic Clouds benefit from a wealth of data across the electromagnetic spectrum, but extracting extragalactic sources from these crowded fields is a less than straightforward endeavour. We used an unsupervised machine learning algorithm (t-distributed stochastic neighbourhood embedding; t-SNE) to classify 6,652 and 1,356 sources in the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, respectively, that were detected in the VISTA Survey of the Magellanic Clouds (VMC) and the Evolutionary Map of the Universe (EMU) survey with the Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder (ASKAP). Multi-wavelength photometry and colours from optical to radio were used as features to cluster similar sources together in 2D space on a t-SNE map. We used previously classified sources to separate the clusters into five classes: AGN, low-redshift galaxies, blazars, dusty stellar objects (e.g. young stellar objects, planetary nebulæ etc) and high proper-motion stars. Previous photometric classifications from the literature match with specific clusters identified, as well as provide insight on areas of the t-SNE map for which there are no previous classifications. This work shows that the combination of unsupervised machine learning with photometry from optical to radio has proven adept at separating the stellar from the extragalactic, and the AGN from the galaxies. Our associated new spectroscopy with SALT includes new discoveries of AGN up to redshift 3.3 and Magellanic emission-line objects.

title: Identification of extragalactic radio sources in the VISTA survey of the Magellanic Clouds using an unsupervised machine learning algorithm

abstract: We produce a measurement of the growth index, $γ$, which is used to parametrize the scale-independent growth of linear matter perturbations on sub-horizon scales, for the $w_0w_a$CDM background model. In 2023, assuming the $Λ$CDM background, the value $γ=0.633^{+0.025}_{-0.024}$ was obtained, excluding the General Relativity value of $γ=0.55$ at $3.7σ$ statistical significance. In 2025, an analysis of baryon acoustic oscillation data from the Dark Energy Spectroscopy Instrument (DESI) demonstrated a preference for a dynamical dark energy over the cosmological constant model, $Λ$, ranging from $2.8-4.2σ$, depending on the external datasets used. Therefore it is important to determine how the $γ$ measurement is modified in the context of dynamical dark energy and verify whether the tension with the expected theoretical value persists. Considering data from Planck cosmic microwave background anisotropies, $fσ_{8}$, baryon acoustic oscillation from DESI and supernova Ia luminosity distances from Phanteon+, we find $γ_{w_0w_a}=0.633\pm0.024$, essentially the same value found for the $Λ$CDM background. This result excludes the General Relativity value for the $w_0w_a$CDM background evolution at $3.4σ$ level. We also show that the $γ$ posteriors across many datasets combinations are consistent with each other and that main driver of the "$γ$ tension" is the $fσ_{8}$ dataset.
